rules.statement: A `client_credentials` access token must carry a `sub` claim set to the client's own server-generated principal identifier, never the raw `client_id` and never a pairwise-projected value.
rules.why: RFC 9068 §2.2 requires `sub` in every JWT access token and, when there is no resource owner, requires it to identify the client; role assignments name the principal, and a `client_id` is chosen by operators and would let a recreated client inherit an earlier client's authority.
rules.check: Look for client-credentials token issuance that omits `sub`, sets it to `client_id` or to a `<client_id>@clients`-style value, or runs it through pairwise subject projection.

rules.statement: A principal identifier that authority attaches to must be generated by the store when the entity is added (16 random bytes, Base64Url), must overwrite any value the caller supplies, and must never change afterwards.
rules.why: Otherwise a caller could pick another actor's principal, and a recreated entity with the same external id would inherit the earlier entity's authority.
rules.check: Look for add/update paths that keep a caller-supplied principal id, derive it from a name or client_id, or let an update change it.

rules.statement: When an entity that owns a principal is removed, remove every role assignment that principal holds in the same operation.
rules.why: Leftover assignments would keep granting authority to a principal that no longer exists.
rules.check: Look for delete paths for clients or other principal-bearing entities that don't also delete the principal's role assignments.

rules.statement: Decide whether a caller is a client acting for itself only through the shared, replaceable client-principal resolver; an endpoint, handler or audit recorder must not compare a token's subject with a client's principal itself.
rules.why: A host that registers its own resolver must get the same answer at authorization, auditing, token exchange and UserInfo; an inline comparison would disagree with it.
rules.check: Look for code comparing `sub` with a client's principal id or `client_id` directly instead of calling the resolver.

rules.statement: A resolver of the acting client must answer each caller (tenant, subject, client_id) once per request, memoizing the answer, including a negative one, in `HttpContext.Items` and not reading the store again for a caller it has answered.
rules.why: Several places in one request ask the same question, and the audit recorder asks after commit, when a self-deleted client is gone from the store; one memoized answer keeps them consistent and avoids repeated reads.
rules.check: Look for resolver implementations that re-read the store or open a new store manager per call, or that memoize only positive answers.

rules.statement: Resolve the acting principal of a request when the caller is authenticated, before the endpoint runs, and have authorization and auditing reuse that answer instead of resolving it in each handler or in the audit recorder.
rules.why: A handler that forgets would record the wrong actor, and the recorder's first read can come after the change is committed, when the actor may no longer exist.
rules.check: Look for new handlers or audit code that look up the acting client or principal themselves rather than reading the answer from the authentication step.

rules.statement: A disabled client's subject must resolve to no principal, so disabling a client withdraws its authority at once, and a client's own subject must never be provisioned or read as a federated or upstream user identity.
rules.why: Authority must stop when the client is disabled, and a client principal is not an end user.
rules.check: Look for principal resolution that ignores the client's enabled flag or that falls through to federated-principal provisioning for a client subject.

rules.statement: Token exchange must reject a client's own token as `subject_token` with `invalid_grant` while still accepting it as `actor_token`, and UserInfo must reject a client's own token with `invalid_token`.
rules.why: A token with no resource owner names no user to exchange for or to describe (RFC 8693, OpenID Connect UserInfo).
rules.check: Look at token exchange and UserInfo changes for the error codes used on a client-acting-for-itself token, and for code that wrongly refuses it as an actor token.

rules.statement: Derive management authority from role assignments read from the store at request time, not from a role or grant-type claim carried on the access token.
rules.why: A role claim is stale until the token expires and names no node of the resource hierarchy, and a grant-type claim is non-standard when the server can decide from its own data.
rules.check: Look for authorization code that reads roles or grant types from token claims to decide management authority.

rules.statement: An authorization check on a resource route must answer `403` to a caller without authority whether or not the resource exists.
rules.why: Answering differently for unknown resources would leak their existence to unauthorized callers.
rules.check: Look for routes that return `404` before checking authority, or that skip the authority check when the resource lookup fails.
